Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Understanding Ethereum Networks
Understanding Ethereum Networks
How Mainnet, testnets, and local blockchains fit into your smart contract workflow.
In this lesson

Learn the purpose of each network type, how gas fees change choices, and the hands-on steps to configure Hardhat for Sepolia.

Why it matters
Choosing the wrong network risks lost funds, wasted time, or missing critical integration issues with wallets and services.
Explore Key Topics
Mainnet
Live network where real ETH moves; highest risk and cost.
Testnets
Public sandboxes using test ETH for safe end-to-end checks.
Local
Fast, resettable blockchains for unit tests and development.
Overview Map
Mainnet
Live chain. Real ETH. Production-ready deployments.
Sepolia / Goerli
Public testnets that mimic Mainnet but use test ETH.

Hardhat, Ganache, Anvil for fast local iteration and unit tests.

We will cover Mainnet risks, testnet choices, local networks, gas economics, the Hardhat configuration, and a short hands-on checklist.

screens.title: Ethereum Mainnet: definition and risks
screens.narratorSegment: The Ethereum Mainnet is the live, public, permissionless blockchain where real ETH and real value are exchanged. When you deploy a contract to Mainnet you publish immutable code that anyone can interact with and every transaction consumes real ETH as gas. That makes Mainnet necessary for production-grade dApps, but it also raises financial and security stakes. A single deployment mistake or vulnerability can cause irreversible loss. A concrete example: deploying a token contract to Mainnet means minting or transferring tokens will cost ETH for each transaction and those tokens may be tradable immediately. Because of the cost and permanence, developers almost always use Mainnet only after rigorous local testing, testnet staging, and third-party audits. A common misconception is that Mainnet simply equals a larger test environment; it does not. Mainnet differs in network participants, real economic incentives, and exposure to front-running, bots, and users you cannot control. Your takeaway is to treat Mainnet as the final, audited release step: budget gas, lock down keys, and verify that all dependencies and oracles behave correctly in production-like tests before going live. Which protection will you add before your next Mainnet deployment?

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Ethereum Mainnet
Definition
Ethereum Mainnet

The live, public blockchain where transactions use real ETH and contracts are globally visible and immutable.

Use case
Production dApps and assets carrying real value.
Risk
Irreversible cost and exposure to attacks if not fully tested.
Misconception
Treating Mainnet as a testing ground ignores economic incentives and real users; it is not a sandbox.
Concrete example
Deploying a token contract on Mainnet will require ETH for deployment and each token transfer will cost gas. Any error becomes public and costly to fix.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Mainnet is for production. Only deploy there after robust local and testnet verification, gas budgeting, and audits.

Quick safety checklist
  • Use a production wallet with planned funding.
  • Confirm configuration in hardhat.config.js and .env.
  • Run a final audit and gas estimate before deploying.

screens.title: Public Testnets: Sepolia and Goerli
screens.narratorSegment: Public testnets are public blockchains that behave like Mainnet but use test ETH to remove financial risk. Developers deploy and exercise contracts on testnets to validate integration with wallets, oracles, and front-ends under network latency similar to Mainnet. Sepolia is currently the recommended long-term public testnet, providing a stable environment for staging. Goerli exists but is being deprecated, so new projects should prefer Sepolia for future-proof testing. A concrete scenario: after unit tests pass locally, you deploy the same compiled contracts to Sepolia and sign transactions with a test wallet funded by a faucet; this confirms your front-end wallet flows and any multi-contract interactions. Testnets do not eliminate all differences: network participants on testnets are fewer and some production services may behave differently. A common mistake is to assume testnet gas behaves exactly like Mainnet; price and miner behavior can differ. The bottom line: use testnets for realistic integration testing and replicate as many production conditions as practical before moving to Mainnet. Which testnet will you use to validate end-to-end behavior for your next release? Public Testnets: Sepolia and Goerli means use sepolia for public staging to validate integrations without real eth.. In practical terms, how public testnets mirror mainnet and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Public Testnets
What they are
Public Testnets

Public networks like Sepolia and Goerli mirror Mainnet behavior but use test ETH so you can deploy and test without monetary risk.

Sepolia
Recommended long-term public testnet for staging and integration testing.
Goerli
Operational but being deprecated; avoid starting new projects here.
Concrete example
After passing local tests, deploy the same contract bytecode to Sepolia, fund a test wallet from a faucet, and exercise UI flows to validate wallet interactions and timing under public network conditions.
Common mistake
Assuming testnet gas and miner behavior exactly match Mainnet. Testnets help but do not perfectly replicate all production conditions.
Key Takeaway

Use Sepolia as your staging ground to verify integrations and reduce risk before Mainnet deployment.

screens.title: Local Development Networks
screens.narratorSegment: Local development networks run entirely on your machine and are essential for fast iteration. Tools like Hardhat Network, Ganache, and Anvil simulate a blockchain with instant transaction confirmations, unlimited test ETH, and the ability to reset state. This makes them ideal for unit tests and rapid debugging cycles. For example, when you run npx hardhat test, Hardhat spins up a local node, deploys contracts, executes tests, and tears down the environment in milliseconds. That speed significantly shortens your feedback loop compared with testnets or Mainnet. However, local networks intentionally trade realism for speed: they do not fully replicate network latency, miner behavior, or the exact gas dynamics you will see on public networks. A common misconception is treating local tests as sufficient for final release checks; always follow local testing with public testnet staging. Use local networks for logic correctness, unit coverage, and developer convenience, then use Sepolia for integration and Mainnet for production. The practice pattern is clear: code and unit test locally, deploy to Sepolia to validate integration, then deploy to Mainnet after audits and budget checks. What will you test locally first in your next contract?

screens.title: A network-based workflow for smart contracts
screens.narratorSegment: A disciplined workflow reduces risk. Start with a local development cycle: write contract code, run unit tests on Hardhat Network, and iterate until logic and basic edge cases are handled. Next, deploy to a public testnet such as Sepolia to validate integrations — wallets, oracles, and front-end flows — and to measure gas under public conditions. After testnet verification, perform audits and formal reviews. Finally, deploy to Mainnet with a carefully prepared deployment script, gas budget, and production wallet. For a concrete sequence: 1) local tests and linting; 2) run automated tests and coverage locally; 3) deploy to Sepolia via hardhat scripts and test real user interactions; 4) run a final staging review and audit; 5) deploy to Mainnet with an incremental rollout strategy and monitoring. A typical misconception is skipping the testnet step because local tests passed; that misses integration issues visible only on public networks. This staged progression keeps cost and risk manageable while increasing confidence at each step. Before you proceed, ask: which test scenarios can only be validated on Sepolia for my dApp? A network-based workflow for smart contracts means follow a stepwise workflow: local development, public testnet staging, audit, then mainnet deployment.. In practical terms, stage, test, and release: a recommended network progression. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Gas Fees: what they are and why they matter
screens.narratorSegment: Gas fees are the units of cost you pay in ETH to execute transactions and deploy contracts on Ethereum. Gas measures computational effort: more complex operations, larger contracts, and storage writes consume more gas. On Mainnet, these fees are paid with real ETH and fluctuate based on network congestion and gas price. Testnets use play ETH from faucets so you can pay gas without financial loss, but public network conditions may still affect transaction timing. Local networks typically simulate gas but give unlimited or free ETH, which accelerates testing but does not reveal true cost trade-offs. A concrete example: deploying a complex contract with many storage variables will require more gas than a smaller contract, so optimizing storage layout or packing variables can significantly reduce Mainnet deployment cost. A common misconception is that gas matters only for transactions; in practice, deployment gas and per-transaction gas both affect long-term costs and design choices. Your practical goal is to estimate expected gas during staging, run gas reports on testnets, and refactor hotspots before Mainnet to control expenses. What contract operation in your project would you optimize first to lower gas?

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Gas Fees
Definition
Gas fees and computational cost

Gas is paid in ETH to cover the computational work of transactions and deployments. Complex operations cost more gas.

Deployment vs transaction
Both cost gas. Deployment gas is paid once; transaction gas is ongoing.
Network differences
Mainnet uses real ETH and fluctuating prices; testnets use faucet ETH and may not match Mainnet congestion.
Concrete example
A large contract with many storage writes can cost significantly more to deploy than a minimal implementation. Simple refactors like packing variables lower gas usage.
Pro tip
Generate gas reports during deployment scripts and compare results between local, Sepolia, and a Mainnet estimate before finalizing design.
Key Takeaway

Gas shapes design decisions. Use staging to estimate costs and optimize expensive operations before Mainnet.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety measures
screens.narratorSegment: Several common mistakes repeatedly cause costly errors. The first is accidentally deploying to Mainnet instead of a testnet. This mistake consumes real ETH and publishes an unreviewed contract. A second mistake is testing with a wallet that contains production funds; always use separate test wallets supplied only with test ETH. A third mistake is storing private keys insecurely in source control. Prevent these issues by using environment variables for RPC URLs and private keys, and by keeping separate configuration blocks per network in hardhat. config. js. Another useful safety measure is to include a final pre-deploy check in your deployment scripts that prints the target network name and confirms a tester-only approval before broadcasting. For example, require an environment variable like DEPLOY_CONFIRM=true for Mainnet runs. A misconception to watch for is assuming that a missing private key prevents accidental Mainnet transactions; in practice, misconfigured providers or scripts can still sign with a local unlocked account. Your next step is to adopt a checklist: confirm network selection, use a test wallet on testnets, audit code, and double-check environment variables. What safety step will you implement first?

Example snippet
// hardhat.config.js
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox");
require("dotenv").config(); // Load environment variables

const SEPOLIA_RPC_URL = process.env.SEPOLIA_RPC_URL || "https://eth-sepolia.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_ALCHEMY_API_KEY";
const PRIVATE_KEY = process.env.PRIVATE_KEY || "YOUR_TEST_WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY";

module.exports = {
  solidity: "0.8.20",
  networks: {
    hardhat: {
      // local settings
    },
    sepolia: {
      url: SEPOLIA_RPC_URL,
      accounts: PRIVATE_KEY !== undefined ? [PRIVATE_KEY] : [],
      chainId: 11155111, // Sepolia's chain ID
    },
  },
};
Note: Replace placeholders in .env and never commit the file.

screens.title: Testing and iteration cadence
screens.narratorSegment: Testing should progress from unit to integration with clear iteration cadence. Begin with unit tests on local networks to validate isolated contract logic and edge cases. Use continuous integration to run these tests on every commit so regressions are detected early. Next, deploy to Sepolia for integration testing: simulate user flows with wallets, multi-contract interactions, and any third-party services. Monitor gas usage and timing to detect issues that unit tests cannot show. Iterate on code, re-run local tests, and repeat testnet deployments as needed. Local networks let you reset state and run many scenarios quickly; public testnets reveal cross-service problems and wallet interactions. A misconception is relying solely on deterministic unit tests and skipping integration tests; this can miss real-world concerns such as oracle latency, front-end wallet behavior, or dependency timeouts. A practical cadence is: local unit tests on every change, scheduled Sepolia runs for larger integration checks, and a final pre-audit staging run. This cadence shortens the feedback loop while keeping the broader system behavior visible. What will you automate first in your testing cadence? screens.title: Wallets, faucets, and external services
screens.narratorSegment: Wallets and external services often behave differently when connected to a public network versus a local mock. Testnets provide the bridge to validate these interactions. For example, MetaMask connections, wallet approvals, and user flows can be exercised only in a public environment where the wallet can request network status and simulate real user events. Faucets exist on public testnets to provide free test ETH so wallets can sign transactions and cover gas. External services like oracles and relayers may also be available or behave differently on public testnets, making Sepolia important for true end-to-end checks. A common misconception is that mocking a wallet locally covers all edge cases; it does not. Browser extensions and wallets often have network-specific UI and permission flows that need to be validated in a live public network. Practical steps include connecting your test wallet to Sepolia, requesting faucet ETH, and running full UI flows to confirm signatures, transaction states, and timeouts. This practice reduces surprises when you move to Mainnet and uncovers integration issues that are invisible in isolated unit tests. Which external service will you validate on Sepolia first?

screens.narratorSegment: Before Mainnet deployment, complete a final set of operational checks. First, ensure a formal security review or audit has been performed for contracts that will hold value. Fourth, plan a rollback or upgrade path using upgradeable proxies if your architecture requires it, understanding that Mainnet contracts are immutable unless designed for upgrades. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll build a mental model of the Ethereum ecosystem so you can pick the right environment for each development stage. Ethereum is not a single playground: the Mainnet is the live, public ledger where real ETH and value move. Testnets replicate Mainnet behavior but use test ETH so you can experiment without financial risk. Local networks run on your machine, giving immediate feedback, resets, and unlimited test ETH for fast iteration. We'll show how these environments fit into a typical workflow: start locally for coding and unit tests, move to a public testnet like Sepolia for integration and wallet testing, and finally deploy to Mainnet when your contract is audited and ready. You will also learn why gas fees matter and how they influence the timing of deployments. Throughout the lesson you will see concrete examples: using Hardhat's local network for rapid tests, requesting test ETH from a faucet on Sepolia, and updating hardhat. config. js to connect to a remote RPC. By the end you'll be able to explain the risks and trade-offs, avoid common deployment mistakes, and choose the right network for your next release. Which environment will you use first on your current project?

By the end of this chapter you will clearly differentiate between Mainnet, public testnets, and local development networks and decide which to use at each stage of development. You will also be able to explain why testnets exist, how to get test ETH from a faucet, and what limited behaviors to expect on each public testnet. Third, you'll learn how to set up and use a local development network for unit tests and rapid iteration, including the advantages of instant confirmations and resettable state. Finally, you will understand gas fees as an operational cost that affects when and how you deploy and how to avoid accidental Mainnet deployments. Each objective connects to a verified competency: configure Hardhat for Sepolia, run local tests, and make an informed deployment plan that includes gas budgeting and safety checks. These are practical skills: you will not only be able to name the networks, but to use them correctly and safely when developing, testing, and releasing smart contracts. Think about a current project and which of these objectives would change your next deployment decision.

These objectives continue with practical verification steps you should practice. First, configure Hardhat to target both the local Hardhat Network and a public testnet like Sepolia using environment variables for RPC URLs and private keys. This prevents accidental exposure of sensitive keys and makes it easier to switch networks during development. Second, run unit tests locally and then run the same deployment script on Sepolia to validate wallet integrations, external services, and gas behavior under realistic latency. Third, learn to read gas usage in transaction receipts and consider simple contract changes to reduce cost, such as packing storage or reducing unnecessary external calls. Finally, adopt safety checks: separate wallets per environment, review hardhat. config. js for target network, and use a test account with only test ETH when interacting with testnets. These skills form a practical checklist for moving from development to staging to production with control and repeatability. Practice them on a small contract and reflect on which step gave you the most confidence.

The Ethereum Mainnet is the live, public, permissionless blockchain where real ETH and real value are exchanged. When you deploy a contract to Mainnet you publish immutable code that anyone can interact with and every transaction consumes real ETH as gas. That makes Mainnet necessary for production-grade dApps, but it also raises financial and security stakes. A single deployment mistake or vulnerability can cause irreversible loss. A concrete example: deploying a token contract to Mainnet means minting or transferring tokens will cost ETH for each transaction and those tokens may be tradable immediately. Because of the cost and permanence, developers almost always use Mainnet only after rigorous local testing, testnet staging, and third-party audits. A common misconception is that Mainnet simply equals a larger test environment; it does not. Mainnet differs in network participants, real economic incentives, and exposure to front-running, bots, and users you cannot control. Your takeaway is to treat Mainnet as the final, audited release step: budget gas, lock down keys, and verify that all dependencies and oracles behave correctly in production-like tests before going live. Which protection will you add before your next Mainnet deployment?

Public testnets are public blockchains that behave like Mainnet but use test ETH to remove financial risk. Developers deploy and exercise contracts on testnets to validate integration with wallets, oracles, and front-ends under network latency similar to Mainnet. Sepolia is currently the recommended long-term public testnet, providing a stable environment for staging. Goerli exists but is being deprecated, so new projects should prefer Sepolia for future-proof testing. A concrete scenario: after unit tests pass locally, you deploy the same compiled contracts to Sepolia and sign transactions with a test wallet funded by a faucet; this confirms your front-end wallet flows and any multi-contract interactions. Testnets do not eliminate all differences: network participants on testnets are fewer and some production services may behave differently. A common mistake is to assume testnet gas behaves exactly like Mainnet; price and miner behavior can differ. The bottom line: use testnets for realistic integration testing and replicate as many production conditions as practical before moving to Mainnet. Which testnet will you use to validate end-to-end behavior for your next release? Public Testnets: Sepolia and Goerli means use sepolia for public staging to validate integrations without real eth.. In practical terms, how public testnets mirror mainnet and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Local development networks run entirely on your machine and are essential for fast iteration. Tools like Hardhat Network, Ganache, and Anvil simulate a blockchain with instant transaction confirmations, unlimited test ETH, and the ability to reset state. This makes them ideal for unit tests and rapid debugging cycles. For example, when you run npx hardhat test, Hardhat spins up a local node, deploys contracts, executes tests, and tears down the environment in milliseconds. That speed significantly shortens your feedback loop compared with testnets or Mainnet. However, local networks intentionally trade realism for speed: they do not fully replicate network latency, miner behavior, or the exact gas dynamics you will see on public networks. A common misconception is treating local tests as sufficient for final release checks; always follow local testing with public testnet staging. Use local networks for logic correctness, unit coverage, and developer convenience, then use Sepolia for integration and Mainnet for production. The practice pattern is clear: code and unit test locally, deploy to Sepolia to validate integration, then deploy to Mainnet after audits and budget checks. What will you test locally first in your next contract?

A disciplined workflow reduces risk. Start with a local development cycle: write contract code, run unit tests on Hardhat Network, and iterate until logic and basic edge cases are handled. Next, deploy to a public testnet such as Sepolia to validate integrations — wallets, oracles, and front-end flows — and to measure gas under public conditions. After testnet verification, perform audits and formal reviews. Finally, deploy to Mainnet with a carefully prepared deployment script, gas budget, and production wallet. For a concrete sequence: 1) local tests and linting; 2) run automated tests and coverage locally; 3) deploy to Sepolia via hardhat scripts and test real user interactions; 4) run a final staging review and audit; 5) deploy to Mainnet with an incremental rollout strategy and monitoring. A typical misconception is skipping the testnet step because local tests passed; that misses integration issues visible only on public networks. This staged progression keeps cost and risk manageable while increasing confidence at each step. Before you proceed, ask: which test scenarios can only be validated on Sepolia for my dApp? A network-based workflow for smart contracts means follow a stepwise workflow: local development, public testnet staging, audit, then mainnet deployment.. In practical terms, stage, test, and release: a recommended network progression. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Gas fees are the units of cost you pay in ETH to execute transactions and deploy contracts on Ethereum. Gas measures computational effort: more complex operations, larger contracts, and storage writes consume more gas. On Mainnet, these fees are paid with real ETH and fluctuate based on network congestion and gas price. Testnets use play ETH from faucets so you can pay gas without financial loss, but public network conditions may still affect transaction timing. Local networks typically simulate gas but give unlimited or free ETH, which accelerates testing but does not reveal true cost trade-offs. A concrete example: deploying a complex contract with many storage variables will require more gas than a smaller contract, so optimizing storage layout or packing variables can significantly reduce Mainnet deployment cost. A common misconception is that gas matters only for transactions; in practice, deployment gas and per-transaction gas both affect long-term costs and design choices. Your practical goal is to estimate expected gas during staging, run gas reports on testnets, and refactor hotspots before Mainnet to control expenses. What contract operation in your project would you optimize first to lower gas?

Several common mistakes repeatedly cause costly errors. The first is accidentally deploying to Mainnet instead of a testnet. This mistake consumes real ETH and publishes an unreviewed contract. A second mistake is testing with a wallet that contains production funds; always use separate test wallets supplied only with test ETH. A third mistake is storing private keys insecurely in source control. Prevent these issues by using environment variables for RPC URLs and private keys, and by keeping separate configuration blocks per network in hardhat. config. js. Another useful safety measure is to include a final pre-deploy check in your deployment scripts that prints the target network name and confirms a tester-only approval before broadcasting. For example, require an environment variable like DEPLOY_CONFIRM=true for Mainnet runs. A misconception to watch for is assuming that a missing private key prevents accidental Mainnet transactions; in practice, misconfigured providers or scripts can still sign with a local unlocked account. Your next step is to adopt a checklist: confirm network selection, use a test wallet on testnets, audit code, and double-check environment variables. What safety step will you implement first?

Wallets and external services often behave differently when connected to a public network versus a local mock. Testnets provide the bridge to validate these interactions. For example, MetaMask connections, wallet approvals, and user flows can be exercised only in a public environment where the wallet can request network status and simulate real user events. Faucets exist on public testnets to provide free test ETH so wallets can sign transactions and cover gas. External services like oracles and relayers may also be available or behave differently on public testnets, making Sepolia important for true end-to-end checks. Let's close with three concise ideas to keep in mind. First, the Ethereum Mainnet is the live production environment where real ETH is used; deploy there only after thorough testing and audits. Second, public testnets like Sepolia provide a realistic public environment using faucet ETH; use them for integration and wallet testing before Mainnet. Third, local development networks such as Hardhat Network or Ganache accelerate development with instant confirmations and resettable state, but they are not substitutes for public staging. Together these environments form a progression from fast iteration to realistic staging to final production. Keep separate wallets and environment-specific configurations to avoid mistakes, estimate gas costs before Mainnet, and perform audits and monitoring as part of your deployment plan.
